newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM may get probation in radioactive freight scare.
newsitem.headline: KLM may get probation in radioactive freight scare.

text.p: The Dutch transport ministry said on Sunday it was considering putting Dutch carrier KLM on probation after the airline flouted legal regulations on transporting radioactive materials.

A ministry spokesman said that KLM's failure to conduct the required inspection of a cargo of radioactive medical equipment submitted by a Dutch firm for shipment constituted a "serious violation" of legal procedures.
"The ministry is weighing the conditional withdrawal of KLM's permit to transport hazardous, particularly radioactive, materials," spokesman Henk Houtman said.
He said the case, which concerned a radioactive cargo carried on board KLM's May 2 KL129 passenger flight to London, was due to be heard on Tuesday.

The ministry would then decide whether to put KLM on probation for a period yet to be determined, during which time a second offence would lead to the carrier's permit being lastingly withdrawn, Houtman said.

The cargo was monitored on arrival in London during routine checks by Britain's Civil Aviation Authority and found to be emitting higher levels of radiation than those indicated in its freight documents, Houtman said.

He said the fault had started at the Petten-based company submitting the cargo for shipment, which had not packaged the equipment properly and had subsequently failed to measure the levels of radiation being emitted.
KLM in turn had not carried out the required acceptance checks, he said.
The airline later failed to notify the Dutch aviation authorities of the higher-than-reported levels of radiation detected by Britain's inspectors.
A KLM spokeswoman said on Sunday that the cargo's levels of radioactivity had at no time exceeded Dutch or European safety norms.
"There was absolutely no cause for concern, given that the actual levels of radiation (found by British and Dutch inspectors) were well below any legal norms or limits," Marjolein Wenting said.

But Houtman said that a probe by Dutch health authorities indicated that the level of radiation absorbed by passengers sitting directly over the cargo during the one-hour flight would have equalled the maximum annual dose considered safe.
"As such it becomes very difficult to say whether or not safety norms have been breached," he said.

Citing confidential documents, Britain's Observer newspaper said on Sunday the cargo had been stowed in the plane's hold just below the galley and rows six and seven, where mainly British and American passengers were seated. ((-- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000, Fax +31 20 504 5040))
